definition:
A Computational Substrate is a 7-tuple:

  𝒮 = (𝒳, 𝒴, ℛ, D, V, E, Φ)

where:

  𝒳 — State Space
    The set of all possible computational inputs.
    Formally: 𝒳 = {0,1}^d for some dimension d ∈ ℕ.
    [IMPLEMENTED] In all tested systems, 𝒳 is the set of d-bit vectors.

  𝒴 — Observation Space
    The set of possible outcomes.
    Formally: 𝒴 = {0,1} (Boolean).
    [IMPLEMENTED] All tested systems produce Boolean outcomes.

  ℛ — Representation Space
    A set of compact representations ("laws") such that each r ∈ ℛ
    defines a function r̂: 𝒳 → 𝒴.
    Formally: ℛ is a language (e.g., GF(2) expressions, DSL programs,
    DFA transition tables) with an interpretation function ⟦·⟧: ℛ → (𝒳 → 𝒴).
    [IMPLEMENTED] ℛ = {GF(2) laws} ∪ {Walsh laws} ∪ {DFA laws} ∪ {DSL programs}.

  D — Discovery Operator
    D: 2^(𝒳×𝒴) → ℛ ∪ {⊥}
    Takes a set of observations O ⊆ 𝒳 × 𝒴 and returns either:
      - a representation r ∈ ℛ such that ⟦r⟧(x_i) = y_i for all (x_i, y_i) ∈ O
      - ⊥ (UNKNOWN / NOT FOUND) if no r ∈ ℛ fits
    [IMPLEMENTED] D = classify() which tries GF(2), Walsh, DFA, and
    program synthesis in order.

  V — Verification Operator
    V: ℛ × 2^(𝒳×𝒴) × (𝒳 → 𝒴) → {accept, reject}
    Takes a representation r, observations O, and (optionally) the true
    function f: 𝒳 → 𝒴, and returns accept or reject.
    [IMPLEMENTED] V = LawVerificationLayer (MDL + AIC + held-out + adversarial).

  E — Execution Operator
    E: ℛ × 𝒳 → 𝒴
    Executes the representation on a new input.
    E(r, x) = ⟦r⟧(x)
    [IMPLEMENTED] E = evaluate_representation() / evaluate_program().

  Φ — Economic Cost Model
    Φ: (D, V, E, O, n) → ℝ
    Computes the net computational advantage:
      Φ = n · (C_direct - C_E) - C_D - C_V
    where:
      C_direct = cost of one direct computation (≈ d)
      C_E = cost of executing a law (≈ |r|)
      C_D = cost of discovery
      C_V = cost of verification
      n = number of predictions
    [IMPLEMENTED] Φ = break_even computation in benchmarks.

A1_Consistency.statement: For all r ∈ ℛ and all (x,y) ∈ O: if D(O) = r, then ⟦r⟧(x) = y.
A1_Consistency.meaning: A discovered law must be consistent with all observations.
A1_Consistency.tag: [DERIVED] Without consistency, D is meaningless — it returns laws that contradict the data.

A2_Generalization.statement: If V accepts r, then for all x ∈ 𝒳: ⟦r⟧(x) = f(x) (where f is the true function).
A2_Generalization.meaning: A verified law must be correct on ALL inputs, not just observed ones.
A2_Generalization.tag: [DERIVED] This is the difference between memorization and law discovery. Without it, the substrate is just a cache.

A3_Compactness.statement: For all r ∈ ℛ: |r| < |O| (the representation is smaller than the raw observation data).
A3_Compactness.meaning: The law must be more compact than the data it explains.
A3_Compactness.tag: [DERIVED] Without compactness, the substrate stores more data than direct computation. This is the MDL principle.

A4_Escalation.statement: If D(O) = ⊥ or V rejects r, then the substrate executes f directly: E(x) = f(x).
A4_Escalation.meaning: When no law is found or verified, the substrate falls back to direct computation.
A4_Escalation.tag: [DERIVED] Without escalation, the substrate would produce wrong answers when it can't find a law. Escalation guarantees correctness.

A5_Amortizability.statement: There exists n* ∈ ℕ such that Φ(D, V, E, O, n*) > 0.
A5_Amortizability.meaning: There exists a prediction volume at which the substrate's net value is positive.
A5_Amortizability.tag: [DERIVED] Not necessary for correctness (A1-A4 guarantee correctness). Necessary for UTILITY — without it, the substrate is pure overhead.

T1_Correctness.statement: Under Axioms A1-A4, the substrate is always correct: for any input x, the substrate's output equals f(x).
T1_Correctness.proof:
Case 1: D(O) = r and V accepts r. By A2 (Generalization), ⟦r⟧(x) = f(x) for all x. E(r,x) = ⟦r⟧(x) = f(x). ✓
Case 2: D(O) = ⊥. By A4 (Escalation), E(x) = f(x). ✓
Case 3: D(O) = r but V rejects r. By A4, E(x) = f(x). ✓
In all cases, the output is f(x). QED.
T1_Correctness.tag: [PROVEN] Correctness follows directly from A2 and A4.
T1_Correctness.counterexample_attempt: No counterexample possible. The proof is by cases and covers all paths.

T2_CompressionBounded.statement: Under Axiom A3, |r| ≥ K(f) where K(f) is the Kolmogorov complexity of f.
T2_CompressionBounded.proof: By definition, K(f) is the length of the shortest program computing f. Any representation r ∈ ℛ that computes f (A2) is a program for f. Therefore |r| ≥ K(f). QED.
T2_CompressionBounded.tag: [PROVEN] This is the Kolmogorov complexity lower bound.
T2_CompressionBounded.counterexample_attempt: No counterexample possible. This is a proven theorem (Li & Vitányi, 2008).

T3_NoUniversalAdvantage.statement: For any substrate 𝒮, if f is drawn uniformly at random from all functions 𝒳 → 𝒴, then E[Φ] ≤ 0.
T3_NoUniversalAdvantage.proof: For a random function f, K(f) ≈ |𝒳| (Chaitin, 1969). By T2, |r| ≥ K(f) ≈ |𝒳|. By A3, |r| < |O|. So |O| > |𝒳| — the substrate needs more observations than the entire state space. Discovery cost ≥ |𝒳|. Savings per prediction = C_direct - C_E ≤ C_direct = d. Break-even n* ≥ |𝒳| / d = 2^d / d → ∞. E[Φ] = n · d - |𝒳| < 0 for any feasible n. QED.
T3_NoUniversalAdvantage.tag: [PROVEN] This is the No Free Lunch theorem (Wolpert, 1996) specialized to computational substrates.
T3_NoUniversalAdvantage.counterexample_attempt: No counterexample possible. This is a proven theorem.

T4_VerificationLimit.statement: If V uses n_adv samples to test r, then P(V accepts r | r is wrong on ε fraction of 𝒳) ≥ (1-ε)^(n_adv).
T4_VerificationLimit.proof: V accepts r if no counterexample is found in n_adv random samples. P(no counterexample in one sample) = 1 - ε. P(no counterexample in n_adv samples) = (1-ε)^(n_adv). This is the sampling limit. QED.
T4_VerificationLimit.tag: [PROVEN] This is the binomial sampling bound.
T4_VerificationLimit.counterexample_attempt: Counterexample: ε = 1/|𝒳| (one wrong state). n_adv = |𝒳|/2. P(miss) = (1 - 1/|𝒳|)^(|𝒳|/2) ≈ e^(-1/2) ≈ 0.6. 60% chance of accepting a wrong law. [MEASURED] in rare exception benchmark.

T5_BreakEvenExists.statement: Under Axioms A1-A4, if D(O) = r and V accepts r, then n* = (C_D + C_V) / (C_direct - C_E) exists and is finite iff C_E < C_direct.
T5_BreakEvenExists.proof: Φ = n · (C_direct - C_E) - (C_D + C_V). Φ > 0 iff n > (C_D + C_V) / (C_direct - C_E). If C_E < C_direct, the denominator is positive and n* is finite. If C_E ≥ C_direct, the denominator is ≤ 0 and no n* exists. QED.
T5_BreakEvenExists.counterexample_attempt: Counterexample: Walsh at d=16. C_D = 2.5M ops, C_direct = 16, C_E = 2. n* = 2.5M / 14 ≈ 178K. State space = 65K. n* > |𝒳| — never amortized. [MEASURED]

GF2.\u211b: Linear functions f(x) = c ⊕ x_{i1} ⊕ ... ⊕ x_{ik}

Walsh.\u211b: Sparse spectral functions (k nonzero Walsh coefficients)

DFA.\u03a6: Depends on DFA size; often not amortized due to large DFA

ProgramSynthesis.\u211b: Programs in Boolean DSL {var, const, not, and, or, xor}
ProgramSynthesis.D: Enumerative search by program size, O(c^k)
ProgramSynthesis.\u03a6: Break-even depends on program size; expensive discovery

PAC_learning.relationship: The substrate IS a PAC-learnable system. Axioms A1-A2 correspond to PAC's consistency and generalization. The verification operator V is a PAC generalization bound.
PAC_learning.tag: [PROVEN] PAC learning (Valiant, 1984) defines exactly this: learn a concept from examples with generalization guarantees.

MDL.relationship: Axiom A3 (Compactness) IS the MDL principle. The substrate's MDL verification stage is a direct application.
MDL.tag: [PROVEN] MDL (Rissanen, 1978) is Axiom A3. The substrate uses MDL as one verification stage.

program_synthesis.relationship: Program synthesis IS the substrate with ℛ = all programs. The substrate is a multi-class synthesizer with verification.

symbolic_regression.relationship: Symbolic regression IS the substrate with ℛ = algebraic expressions. It's program synthesis over a different DSL.
symbolic_regression.tag: [DERIVED] Symbolic regression = program synthesis over arithmetic DSL. Same abstraction.

abstract_interpretation.relationship: Abstract interpretation has no A2 (Generalization) — it over-approximates, doesn't guarantee exact correctness.
abstract_interpretation.tag: [DERIVED] Abstract interpretation violates A2. It's a different (weaker) abstraction.

SAT_SMT.relationship: SAT/SMT solves instances, not discovers universal laws. No A2 (Generalization) — each solve is independent.
SAT_SMT.tag: [DERIVED] SAT/SMT is a subroutine of D, not the full abstraction.

theorem_proving.relationship: Theorem proving with constructive proofs IS program synthesis (Curry-Howard). But theorem proving needs axioms; the substrate needs only observations.
theorem_proving.tag: [DERIVED] Different inputs (axioms vs observations). Same output (proofs/programs).

e_graphs.relationship: E-graphs optimize known expressions. No D (Discovery) — the expression is given, not discovered from observations.
e_graphs.tag: [DERIVED] E-graphs are a subroutine for E (Execution), not the full abstraction.

equality_saturation.relationship: Same as e-graphs — needs a starting expression, not observations.

compiler_optimization.relationship: Compiler optimization transforms source code. No D from observations. Needs source code.
compiler_optimization.tag: [DERIVED] Different problem: optimization vs discovery from observations.

supercompilation.relationship: Supercompilation transforms source code. Same as compiler optimization.

partial_evaluation.relationship: Partial evaluation specializes code given known inputs. No D from observations.

probabilistic_programming.relationship: Probabilistic programming learns distributions, not deterministic laws. No A2 (exact generalization).

category_theory.relationship: Category theory provides a language for structure, not a learning algorithm. No D (Discovery) operator.
category_theory.tag: [DERIVED] Category theory is a language, not a computational substrate.

algorithmic_information_theory.relationship: AIT provides the theoretical foundation (Kolmogorov complexity). T2 and T3 are AIT theorems. But AIT doesn't define D, V, E, Φ.
algorithmic_information_theory.tag: [DERIVED] AIT is the theoretical foundation, not the full abstraction. The substrate uses AIT results (T2, T3) but adds D, V, E, Φ.

final_assessment.relationship: B — equivalent to an existing theory
final_assessment.statement: The Computational Substrate abstraction is equivalent to PAC-learnable MDL-based program synthesis. It is NOT a novel theory.
evidence: [PROVEN] Axioms A1-A2 = PAC learning (Valiant, 1984): consistency + generalization.
[PROVEN] Axiom A4 = standard fallback in any learning system.
[PROVEN] The substrate's D = program synthesis (v6.34 equivalence proof).
[PROVEN] The substrate's V = PAC generalization bound (sampling).
[PROVEN] Theorems T2-T3 are direct consequences of Kolmogorov complexity and No Free Lunch.
[PROVEN] All 4 implemented families (GF2, Walsh, DFA, Synthesis) are instances.
[PROVEN] 4 of 15 existing fields are equivalent (PAC, MDL, Synthesis, Symbolic Regression).
[PROVEN] 11 of 15 fields are NOT equivalent (they violate at least one axiom).
final_assessment.what_is_novel: Nothing in the theory is novel. The NOVELTY is in the ENGINEERING: the specific combination of (a) multiple representation families tried in order of increasing cost, (b) 4-stage verification with adversarial search, and (c) the economic cost model Φ that determines when to use the substrate vs direct computation. This combination is an engineering contribution, not a mathematical one.
final_assessment.what_is_known: PAC learning (1984), MDL (1978), program synthesis (1960s), Kolmogorov complexity (1965), No Free Lunch (1996), Gaussian elimination (1809), Walsh-Hadamard transform (1923), DFA minimization (Moore, 1956), L* algorithm (Angluin, 1987). Every component of the substrate is a known technique.
final_assessment.axiom_independence: Axioms A1-A4 are independent: each can be violated without violating the others. A5 is not independent of A1-A4 (it's a utility condition, not a correctness condition). The axioms are NOT sufficient to guarantee A5 (amortizability) — that depends on the specific function, representation, and cost model.
